transcript.text: Section 4 You will hear part of an environmental
studies lecture about the possibility of using insects as a source of food.
First you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on page 8.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Good morning.
Over the last few weeks we've been talking about the challenges of producing food for
the global population.
And there's been a lot of interest recently in new sources of food and one of the most
interesting is insects.
Well, why should insects be considered as a food source?
Well, for a start a number of them are full of protein and many also have certain vitamins
which may surprise you, more so than a typical farm animal in fact.
And compared to farm animals whose waste products contain a great deal of ammonia, the waste
products of insects are far less acidic and would therefore do very little damage to
the soil or to any of the rivers that run through farmland.
Furthermore, when it comes to the production of insects the expense would be very low.
No trees need to be chopped down or forest turned to pasture so the space that they would
occupy would be radically smaller than for say cows or sheep.
But even if some consumers decided that they'd rather not put insects in their shopping
basket we could also consider how insects might be added to animal feed, the food given
to farm animals.
It's already known that some insects, if they were part of the animal feed, would act
as a sort of natural antibiotic within a cow or sheep's digestive system, thus removing
the need for human intervention.
This would be a cost effective and environmentally friendly alternative for farmers.
However, if consumers do decide that insects are a potential superfood, a way of feeding
the world, then the next question is where do we source them from?
The wild perhaps or should they be bred on insect farms?
Well, if we take from the wild one potential consequence of this is that too many will
be taken and in turn a species could become endangered or extinct.
Then for insects which are harvested from the wild we have no way of knowing where they
have been or what they have come in contact with and this could have harmful consequences
for human health.
Imagine the scenario if food producers or retailers were supplied with insects that were carrying
bacteria, this is not something we want to add to the food chain.
If insects are bred on farms, the problems I've just outlined could be avoided and in
many countries it's already the case that demand for insects is growing, really growing
and it's not in rural areas where you'd expect, but in fact in the cities.
In Thailand for example where the demand has really shot up, however, people in countries
where insects are traditionally what people eat, they'll tell you that when insects are
intensively farmed their taste is simply not the same.
Ironically this is the same accusation that people have when it comes to the way that cows
and sheep are raised.
Insect farmers also face a series of challenges and researchers are keen to assist.
First of all when it comes to breeding different insects have different requirements.
For a start it's essential to maintain a suitable temperature for many species to reproduce.
If this isn't right nothing's going to happen.
Another problem is something that often happens when any species is bred in a confined space
and so far researchers and farmers have not come up with any clear or long term effective
solution to it.
We're talking about the problem of disease.
You don't want a whole colony wiped out in one go.
There's also the question of where insects need to be kept.
If insects are to be bred as a superfood then the tanks used to house them have to be
better designed and this has to happen so that cleaning takes up less time.
If we're talking about mass production we don't want this to be a time consuming activity
and finally like I said before insects have long been part of the diet in some countries
but not so in others.
The farmers want to encourage people in say England or France or Germany to eat insects
then they're going to have to develop a strategy and I'm not talking about production
but marketing.
Something that'll persuade potential customers to try something different.
Well, I've given you a general overview of the situation.
Now let's look at some specific examples.
